PATIENT: Lysander Fairfax Phone: 28451903 email:bradleymorgan@example.org DATE OF BIRTH: 1947-05-12 AGE: 80 years
FOLLOW-UP DATE: 01/19/30 FOLLOWED BY: Dr. Emily Carter
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Worsening shortness of breath, persistent cough with greenish sputum, and increased fatigue.
HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Lysander Fairfax returns for follow-up after one week from his last visit, during which he underwent a repeat chest X-ray and sputum culture. The patient reports that his respiratory symptoms have not improved significantly. He continues to experience severe dyspnea, particularly at rest and during minimal exertion. The productive cough remains unchanged, with greenish sputum that has a strong, foul odor. He reports intermittent fevers, which he attributes to night sweats that have persisted, causing discomfort and distress.
Despite adherence to the prescribed medications, including oral Levofloxacin and Prednisone, Mr. Fairfax states that he feels increasingly fatigued and has difficulty performing activities of daily living. He has noted no improvement in his appetite and is concerned about his ongoing weight loss.
REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General - + significant fatigue, + intermittent fevers, + night sweats, - weight loss. Pulmonary - + persistent productive cough with foul-smelling greenish sputum, + increased wheezing, - hemoptysis. Cardiac - no chest pain, - orthopnea, - paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Gastrointestinal - + decreased appetite, - nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Musculoskeletal - no joint pain. Neurological - no dizziness or headaches.
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs: - Blood Pressure: 128/74 mmHg - Heart Rate: 95 bpm - Respiratory Rate: 30 breaths/min - Oxygen Saturation: 82% on supplemental oxygen (6 L via nasal cannula).
General: The patient appears fatigued and is in moderate to severe respiratory distress, utilizing accessory muscles for breathing.
HEENT: No nasal flaring; oropharynx clear, no signs of dehydration.
Lungs: Marked wheezing on auscultation; decreased breath sounds bilaterally; prolonged expiration with rhonchi; crackles audible throughout lung fields.
Cardiac: Regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs or gallops; peripheral pulses intact.
Extremities: No edema; no tenderness on palpation.
ASSESSMENT
1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbation with persistent bacterial pneumonia, evidenced by ongoing respiratory symptoms, hypoxemia, and clinical deterioration. 2. Persistent hypoxemia requiring increased supplemental oxygen and consideration of alternative therapeutic interventions. 3. Significant fatigue and decreased functional capacity warranting further evaluation and possible adjustment of treatment regimen.
PLAN
1. Discontinue oral Levofloxacin due to inadequate clinical response; initiate intravenous Piperacillin/Tazobactam 4.5 g every 6 hours to cover for resistant organisms based on sputum culture results. 2. Continue oral Prednisone at 80 mg daily and reassess in 48 hours for response to increased steroid therapy. 3. Increase supplemental oxygen to 8 L via nasal cannula; consider immediate transfer to the respiratory care unit for closer monitoring and potential initiation of non-invasive ventilation (NIV) support. 4. Repeat chest X-ray to assess for any new complications, including potential effusion or worsening pneumonia. 5. Continue nebulized bronchodilator therapy (Albuterol) every four hours as needed and consider adding Ipratropium bromide for synergistic bronchodilation. 6. Schedule a follow-up visit within 48 hours or sooner if symptoms worsen; discuss the possibility of pulmonary rehabilitation following stabilization.
DISPOSITION
Mr. Fairfax remains under close observation in the internal medicine unit with a focus on managing his COPD exacerbation and pneumonia. The treatment team will continue to monitor his respiratory status closely and adjust the treatment plan as needed to improve his clinical condition. The patient is reminded to report any new or worsening symptoms promptly, and education regarding the importance of adherence to the prescribed therapy will be reinforced, especially concerning the new IV antibiotic regimen.
